new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's lexical coding (Bertinetto & Loporcaro 2005: stress distinctive, within last three syllables). Adds the phonological detail that the stressed syllable must be heavy (bimoraic) in standard Italian, with open-syllable lengthening, and penult > antepenult duration, plus the stress-conditioned diphthong alternation. It does not state the three-syllable window or the closed-penult constraint itself.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dissertation gives no placement rule: it takes Italian word stress as lexically given ('lexical stress', marked with accents in the data; orthography marks only final stress, città, caffè) and studies what stress does to the syllable. Its claims: vowel length is not contrastive; a stressed syllable is bimoraic (stress-to-weight), realised by vowel lengthening in open syllables or by a coda; stressed penults are longer than stressed antepenults; the mobile diphthongs [jE]/[wO] occur only under stress and revert to monophthongs when stress shifts under suffixation (buono/bonissimo). It reports, without endorsing, Sluyters' (1992) claim that Italian is quantity-sensitive. The reading 'lexical (unpredictable)' is inferred from its treatment of stress as lexical input, not from an explicit placement statement; confidence low.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only incidental: fn. 79 (p. 84) mentions a careful pronunciation s[o.a]vità 'with secondary stress on the first syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift under suffixation removes the mobile diphthong (cieco/cecone, tuona/tonare); -issimo keeps the diphthong (buonissimo) while -ario attracts stress (bonario). Antepenult-stressed words have shorter stressed vowels (Marotta: consistently only for words with stress on the first syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: Van der Veer (2006) describes standard Italian (his phrase, p. 30) with experimental speakers; Peperkamp's RdL article distinguishes northern vs. southern (Palermo) informants for secondary stress only. No opened work describes a regional dialect as its object.

tone_statements.quote: Si incontra spesso il termine tono anche negli studi relativi a lingue, come l’italiano, nelle quali la variazione di altezza tonale ha valore solo a livello postlessicale, cioè in relazione alla frase (§ 3.4). In questo caso, il termine può indicare uno degli elementi primitivi che compongono i ‘morfemi’ o ‘fonemi’ tonali oppure un elemento di una sequenza distintiva (per es., in italiano, un tono basso caratterizza l’accento tonale principale delle frasi dichiarative neutre, descritto come discendente; si pensi alla pronuncia di mela in Maria mangia una mela).
tone_statements.translation: The term 'tone' is also often met in studies of languages, such as Italian, in which variation in pitch has value only at the post-lexical level, i.e. in relation to the sentence (sec. 3.4). In that case the term may denote one of the primitives making up tonal 'morphemes' or 'phonemes', or an element of a distinctive sequence (e.g., in Italian, a low tone characterises the main pitch accent of neutral declarative sentences, described as falling; think of the pronunciation of mela in Maria mangia una mela).
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone: F0 is distinctive only post-lexically (intonational pitch accents and boundary tones); word prosody is a free, distinctive dynamic stress accent cued mainly by duration.

sources.quote: Italian is a free-stress language [...] Disyllabic words are almost always stressed on the penultimate syllable. With more than two syllables, the situation is more complex, but the dominant pattern, as noted, is still penultimate syllable stress. Indeed, about 77% of Italian words, including all syllable lengths except for monosyllabic words, are stressed on the penultimate syllable and only 18% are stressed on the antepenultimate syllable with the remaining 5% involving words with other stress patterns [...] when stress is placed on the word's final syllable, it is orthographically marked by a diacritic on the vowel (e.g., "coliBRI" 'hummingbird'). Second, when the word's penultimate syllable is heavy (i.e., when it ends with a consonant, e.g., "concerto" 'concert'), it virtually always bears stress, with some rare exceptions such as "MANdorla" 'almond' and "POlizza" 'policy'. [...] In Italian, stress is mainly reflected in duration differences between syllables with primary stress and unstressed syllables.

sources.quote: In Italian, too, the position of the stressed syllable can vary, and is most frequently on one of the last three syllables. However, stress placement in these languages does not follow a strict rule - thus, it is unpredictable. In Italian, there are two main stress patterns: a dominant pattern, on the penultimate syllable, occurring on ~75% of words (e.g., bamBIno, 'child'), and a non-dominant pattern, on the antepenultimate syllable, occurring on ~18% of words (e.g., TAvolo, 'table'; Colombo, 1992; Spinelli, Sulpizio & Burani, 2017). Stress on the last syllable is much less frequent (about 2-3%). The main acoustic correlate of stress in Italian is the increase in duration of the vowel, in particular in open non-final syllables (Bertinetto, 1980; D'Imperio & Rosenthal, 1999).
sources.locator: p. 122 (background section 'Acoustic investigations of the development of stress production'); own finding p. 131 (General Discussion)
sources.note: Acoustic study of vowel duration under stressed/unstressed and singleton/geminate contexts in Italian children and adults (nonwords like /paˈpaso/ vs /ˈpapaso/), giving durational correlates of primary stress.

sources.quote: Stress assignment in Italian polysyllabic words is neither diacritically marked nor predicted by rules. Most three- and four-syllable words are stressed on the penultimate syllable, which is considered as the dominant (or “regular”) stress. Indeed, out of 309 Italian loanwords: - 247 are stressed on the penultimate syllable (79.9%). - 57 are stressed on the antepenultimate syllable (18.4%). - 4 are stressed on the final syllable (1.4%). - 1 case of stress variation is attested (0.3%).

Most three- and four-syllable Italian words are stressed on the penultimate syllable, that is, they carry a dominant stress (e.g., faRIna – "flour"). sources.citation: Jacobs, Haike (1994). How optimal is Italian stress? Linguistics in the Netherlands 11:61-70.
sources.quote: In Italian, apart from cases of final stress which will be discussed below, main stress can be on the penultimate syllable or on the antepenultimate syllable. If the prefinal syllable is heavy, stress is generally on the penult. According to Sluyters (1990:80) only a few lexical entries ignore prefinal heavy syllables by antepenultimately stressing them ... Final stress in Italian occurs in a set of well-defined environments ... a) on word-final heavy syllables (VC, no underlying long vowels) b) on vowel-final stems which do not undergo inflection c) on stressed monosyllables. Final stress in environment (1a) is not obligatory. Penultimate and antepenultimate stress are also possible.
sources.locator: pp. 61-62, sec. 0 and sec. 1 'Italian stress' ( lines 30-80)
sources.note: OT account: main stress on penult or antepenult (final only in listed environments, with exceptions both ways, e.g. festivál/féstival, rósa); heavy penult generally stressed; cornice/calice-type contrasts require unpredictable (lexical) extrametricality; concludes that 'lexical marking of optional or exceptional patterns is inevitabl[e]' (p. 61). Confirms lexical coding and the heavy-penult sub-generalisation.

tone.translation: The term 'tone' is also often met in studies of languages, such as Italian, in which variation in pitch has value only at the post-lexical level, i.e. in relation to the sentence (sec. 3.4). In that case the term may denote one of the primitives making up tonal 'morphemes' or 'phonemes', or an element of a distinctive sequence (e.g., in Italian, a low tone characterises the main pitch accent of neutral declarative sentences, described as falling; think of the pronunciation of mela in Maria mangia una mela).
tone.summary: No lexical tone: F0 is distinctive only post-lexically (intonational pitch accents and boundary tones); word prosody is a free, distinctive dynamic stress accent cued mainly by duration.
